angle: A8-target-methodology — Exceedance methodology, and whether the prediction target itself is right
verdict:
PURSUE, BUT NOTHING HERE IS YET CITABLE. ***THIS ANGLE CONTAINS ZERO VERIFIED CLAIMS.*** Adversarial verification was cut before reaching A8, so all 34 upstream extractions are tier-3 unverified and every finding below carries confidence "unverified". Under the project's own tier-3 rules, none of this may serve as the warrant for a numeric performance figure, an effect size, or the core argument of a recommendation — so this angle currently supplies LEADS ONLY, and every number quoted below (80-98% area underestimation, AUC 0.567/0.482 zero-shot transfer, PSS ratio 0.65, inter-sensor r 0.43-0.81, the CFR and Iowa DNR quotations) must be re-verified against primary sources before it enters any writeup, slide, or design decision. Two of the six sources are 2026 preprints/articles that could not be fully retrieved (Elsevier 403 on Brenning; arXiv figure-read-off numbers on Baggio & Muzy), which is exactly the profile where 'confident overreach from thin evidence' bites.

With that stated, the angle is worth pursuing, for one reason that is structural rather than evidentiary: it is the only angle in this corpus that attacks the between-site gap by CHANGING THE TARGET rather than by finding new features. The project's central problem is that it is 'a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker' (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21; macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24), and seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed. The single highest-value lead here is that the REGULATOR'S OWN DEFINITION OF NITRATE EXCEEDANCE IN IOWA IS A SITE-LEVEL RATE, NOT A DAY-LEVEL EVENT — reportedly a three-year frequency-of-exceedance test binned at 10% and 25% of samples. If that holds on verification, the project has been optimizing a day-level functional while the decision-relevant functional is precisely the between-site quantity it predicts worst. That reframing costs no new data, is evaluable at n=19 independent basin families (19 rate estimates, not 160k rows), and is the one recommendation in this angle that would survive even if most of the numeric claims turn out misstated.

The second-highest-value lead is negative and should temper expectations: the methodological fork the angle was commissioned to resolve — direct binary classification vs regression/distributional-then-threshold — appears, on unverified evidence, to be a NON-ISSUE at this project's base rate. The distributional route's reported advantage is concentrated at rare-event probabilities (p << 0.2) and vanishes at moderate p; the violation base rate is 0.263. Likewise peaks-over-threshold / EVT appears inapplicable: a 26.3% base rate is not a tail. So the answer to question (a) is provisionally 'the current direct-classification choice is fine, do not spend effort switching it,' and effort should go to question (b) — the target definition — instead.

Third: the angle produced NO published virtual-sensor benchmark comparable to LOFO AUC 0.820. The closest spatial-holdout analogue found (beach FIB, zero-shot cross-region AUC 0.567 and 0.482, n=2 effective transfer units) is a different analyte at a far coarser spatial granularity. The evaluation-metric gap is real and cheap to close (BSS/PSS/CSI/HSS against a climatological reference), but the comparator literature it would unlock has not been located. Treat 'we have no external benchmark for our 0.820' as a live, unresolved deficiency of this angle, not as a solved problem.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. The regulatorily meaningful unit of nitrate exceedance in Iowa is reportedly not a day and not a sample but a SITE-LEVEL EXCEEDANCE RATE over a three-year assessment period: Iowa DNR's 2020 assessment methodology is quoted as requiring that 'significantly more than 10% of the samples violate Iowa's Class C criterion for nitrate' before impairment is identified, tested with a binomial small-sample rule (Lin et al. 2000) at >90% confidence. The same document reportedly uses a moving annual AVERAGE for atrazine, indicating the frequency-of-exceedance choice for nitrate is deliberate rather than incidental. IF VERIFIED, this is the most consequential item in the angle: the decision-relevant functional is a site's long-run exceedance rate — exactly the between-site term the model predicts worst (between_rate_r2 0.24 against macro_auc 0.90). The project would be optimizing day-level timing while the regulator scores site-level level. This claim is tier-3 and unverified; the Iowa DNR PDF must be re-read before this framing is asserted anywhere.
findings.effectSize: Reported: 3-year assessment window; >10%-of-samples threshold; >90% confidence; nitrate uses frequency-of-exceedance while co-located atrazine uses a moving annual average. No model-performance effect size — this is a target-definition claim.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable (regulatory document, not a modeling study)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — and uniquely so. Evaluating a predicted site-level exceedance rate needs 19 rate estimates, one per independent basin family, not 160k row-level predictions. n=19 is small for a regression but is the natural sample size for this target rather than a handicap imposed on it. This is the only recommendation in the angle whose evidence requirement shrinks rather than grows under the n=19 constraint.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — predicting an annual/three-year exceedance rate at an arbitrary pin requires no local history, no discharge gauge, and no monitored upstream neighbor. It is strictly easier to deliver than the current daily probability and is arguably what a map-pin product should show.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. Iowa's nitrate assessment outcome is reportedly THREE-CLASS rather than binary, with Table 10 defining Fully Supported as '<10% of the samples violate the ... MCLs (90% CL)', Partially Supported as '>10% to <25%', and Not Supported as '>25% of the samples exceed the MCL(s)', subject to a minimum of 10 samples. IF VERIFIED, this yields a directly actionable, regulator-aligned evaluation for the between-site term: score the model on whether it places an unseen basin family in the correct <10% / 10-25% / >25% bin. That is a 19-unit, three-class confusion matrix — a test the project can actually run today against its existing LOFO folds with no new data, and a far more honest report of site-ranking ability than between_rate_r2 alone. Tier-3; the cut points and the minimum-n rule must be confirmed against the source PDF before use.
findings.effectSize: Reported cut points at 10% and 25% of samples exceeding; minimum n=10 samples for an assessment.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH. A three-class assignment over 19 basin families is a coarse test with wide confidence intervals — a single misbinned family moves accuracy by ~5 points — so it should be reported with exact binomial intervals and never as a headline point estimate. But it is computable now and its power is adequate to distinguish 'ranks sites usefully' from 'ranks sites at chance'.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — bin assignment is derived entirely from predicted exceedance rates, which need only weather and land-use features.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT IN THE ANGLE FOR PRODUCT FRAMING. The 10 mg/L nitrate-N criterion is reportedly a DESIGNATED-USE-SPECIFIC Iowa criterion applying ONLY to Class C waters ('source of a water supply'), with the criterion listed as 'none' for all six aquatic-life classes and for Class A (swimmable) and Class HH; the document is quoted as stating 'At concentrations seen in surface waters, nitrate is not believed to be toxic to aquatic life; thus, there are no water quality criteria ... that apply to aquatic life uses.' Separately, the federal MCL is reportedly defined on TREATED water at the entry point to the distribution system (40 CFR 141.23(a)(2)), so applying 10 mg/L to raw in-stream water is an analogy to a drinking-water standard rather than a regulatory exceedance. IF VERIFIED, a 'violation' prediction at an arbitrary Iowa map pin has NO regulatory meaning unless that segment is Class C designated, and the product must say so in the UI rather than implying a legal exceedance. Tier-3 on both the Iowa Table 6 content and the CFR citation; both are cheap to verify and MUST be verified before any public-facing wording is chosen, because the failure mode here is a legal misstatement, not a modeling error.
findings.effectSize: Reported: 10 mg/L as N applies to 1 of 9 designated-use classes in Iowa Table 6; zero 40 CFR 141 provisions reportedly apply to ambient streams.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable — this is a labeling/communication constraint, not a modeling method. It costs nothing at any n.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: N/A as a method, but it BINDS the ungauged-pin product directly: the pin's designated-use class determines whether the prediction is a regulatory statement or a physical one, and the class is a property of the stream segment, retrievable from the Iowa DNR designated-use GIS layer.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. The closest published analogue to this project's deployment target — zero-shot spatial transfer of a threshold-exceedance classifier to a region with no local labels — reportedly collapsed to near-chance: Random Forests trained on Chicago beaches and applied to San Diego scored AUC 0.567, and San Diego to Chicago scored AUC 0.482, described by the authors as 'no better than chance alone', against same-region AUCs of 0.733 and 0.607 (sensitivity reportedly fell 0.742 -> 0.463 and 0.256 -> 0.208). IF VERIFIED, this corroborates the project's diagnosis that between-site absolute-level transfer is where these models break, and it means LOFO AUC 0.820 is above every cross-region number in that study. But the comparison is weak in three ways that must be stated whenever it is used: different analyte (fecal indicator bacteria, hours-scale coastal response, not tile-drained agricultural nitrate), coarser spatial units (two whole metro regions, i.e. n=2 effective transfer units versus our 19 basin families), and — decisively — tier-3 status. Do NOT present 0.820 as 'beating the literature' on the strength of this. Tier-3 unverified.
findings.effectSize: Reported: local AUC 0.733 (San Diego) / 0.607 (Chicago) vs zero-shot 0.567 and 0.482; sensitivity 0.742 -> 0.463 and 0.256 -> 0.208. 33 beaches, 15,033 beach-days.
findings.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (region-level), per the extraction — this is the one comparable protocol found in the angle, which is why verifying it is high-priority.
findings.nBasins: 33 beaches (19 Chicago freshwater 2016-2019, 14 San Diego marine 2014-2021), but transfer evaluated at region level => n=2 effective independent transfer units.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The study's own n=2 transfer units is a MORE severe version of our constraint, and its authors reportedly could not determine which source sites transfer well. This is a cautionary datum about what n=19 can and cannot establish, not a method to adopt.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The zero-shot setting IS the ungauged-pin setting, so the finding is directly on-target — and its message is that this setting is where performance dies.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND A HARD NEGATIVE FOR ANY TRANSFER-LEARNING PROPOSAL. In the same beach study, the reported headline gain ('28.3% increase in WF1 and 5.4% in AUC') came from SUPERVISED transfer learning that requires labeled exceedance observations AT THE TARGET SITE — the paper is quoted as stating 'The assumption in supervised TL is that a few samples of labeled target data are provided.' The two successful methods (Feature Augmentation, Boosting for Weighted Transfer) are supervised, and the number of target labels required is reportedly NOT stated. Meanwhile CORAL — the UNSUPERVISED domain-adaptation method needing only unlabeled target features, i.e. the one family that would be LEGAL for an arbitrary map pin — reportedly 'never improved performance' in any transfer direction, and SMOTE/ADASYN oversampling reportedly showed 'significant underperformance'. IF VERIFIED: the deployment-legal adaptation methods are exactly the ones that failed, and the ones that worked DO NOT WORK for this product. Transfer learning would only apply to onboarding a NEW MONITORED site after it accumulates observations — a different product. State this prominently if TL is ever proposed. Tier-3 unverified.
findings.effectSize: Reported: Chicago->SD TL-FA AUC 0.713 vs zero-shot 0.567 (local ceiling 0.733); SD->Chicago TL-FA AUC 0.610 vs zero-shot 0.482. TL reportedly RECOVERED local performance but did not exceed it. CORAL: zero improvement in all directions.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Supervised TL is moot here regardless of n, because the target-label requirement disqualifies it. The unsupervised alternative reportedly failed at n=2 regions; at n=19 families there is no reason to expect better and no published evidence either way.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO — explicitly not. Supervised TL requires target-site labels the product does not have. This is a clear-cut case of the deployment constraint killing an otherwise attractive method.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. Regression-then-threshold may be systematically biased for exceedance delineation: Brenning, Frank & Suesse (2026, Environmental Modelling & Software 204:107097) reportedly find that thresholding point predictions of groundwater nitrate UNDERESTIMATES the total threshold-exceeding area by 80%-98%, even for models with 'strong concentration-prediction metrics'. The stated mechanism is shrinkage of conditional-mean/kriged predictions toward the mean, so they systematically fail to cross the threshold. IF VERIFIED, this supports the project's existing choice to make the binary classifier PRIMARY, and — more actionably — it means the REG model (R2 0.328) must NOT be repurposed as a violation detector by thresholding its output at 10 mg/L without recalibration. NOTE THE EVIDENCE QUALITY HONESTLY: this was extracted from the ABSTRACT ONLY; the full text was unreachable (Elsevier 403 on both the HTML article and the CC-BY PDF), the split protocol is unknown, and the number of monitoring units is not recoverable. The 80-98% figure is an unverified abstract number about a static groundwater mapping problem with no time-series component, and must not be quoted as if it applied to this project's stream time series.
findings.effectSize: Reported: 80%-98% underestimation of exceedance area by thresholding point predictions. Abstract-only extraction.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown — the abstract reportedly describes 'target-weighted cross-validation' but does not state a spatial-holdout design, so these numbers are NOT comparable to LOFO AUC 0.820. (The lead author maintains the sperrorest R package and advocates spatial CV, making a spatial design likely but NOT established.)
findings.nBasins: unknown — groundwater wells, national scale, count not recoverable from the abstract; most likely German national groundwater monitoring, itself unverified.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The bias argument is about estimator behavior, not sample size, so it is n-independent in principle. But its empirical support comes from a dense national well network, and nothing establishes that the magnitude carries to 19 basin families.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: PARTIALLY. The estimator-bias argument and the probability-first framing transfer to any setting. The paper's actual modeling stack is reportedly trans-Gaussian regression-kriging + quantile regression forests, with semivariogram practical ranges of 0.3-22.3 km — far shorter than Iowa inter-sensor distances — so the KRIGING half requires a spatially dense observation network and will NOT work at an arbitrary Iowa pin. Only the QRF + calibration half is deployable.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, BUT THE CHEAPEST TESTABLE IDEA IN THE ANGLE. Brenning et al. reportedly propose AREA CALIBRATION as the correction: 'a calibrated probability threshold that ensures an unbiased delineation of the polluted area', where the total exceedance extent is estimated from the data first and the operating probability threshold is then chosen so the predicted positive area matches it; the authors reportedly state this 'effectively eliminates this bias and balances omission versus commission errors' and that the method is model-agnostic. TRANSLATED TO THIS PROJECT: instead of picking the operating point by maximizing F-beta at beta=2 (current: recall 0.864, 59% false alarms), pick the threshold so that the PREDICTED violation rate on held-out folds equals the estimated true base rate 0.263, then report omission vs commission balance. This is a few lines of code against existing LOFO predictions, requires no new data, and is worth running as a diagnostic regardless of whether the source verifies — but the CLAIM THAT IT ELIMINATES BIAS is tier-3, no residual bias figure is recoverable from the abstract, and it must not be presented as an established improvement until the paper is obtained.
findings.effectSize: Reported: bias 'effectively eliminated'; no numeric residual bias recoverable from the abstract.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — rate-matched threshold selection uses aggregate predicted-positive rates, not per-unit estimates, so it is one of the few calibration procedures that does not degrade badly at 19 units. Estimating the 'true' target rate at an unseen basin is itself the between-site problem, so the honest version calibrates to the pooled held-out rate and reports per-family omission/commission spread.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — it is a post-hoc threshold choice on the model's own probability output and needs nothing from the target site.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT ARGUES AGAINST CHANGING THE TARGET. Baggio & Muzy (2026, arXiv:2605.31079) reportedly run the exact fork this angle was commissioned to resolve — direct binary classification of exceedance (M1) versus modeling the full conditional distribution and integrating its tail (M2) — and report M2 better or equal everywhere, with the advantage concentrated at RARE events and the two approaches essentially EQUIVALENT at moderate exceedance probability (reported PSS_1/PSS_2 approaching 1.0 at p=0.2, falling to roughly 0.65 at p=0.002). THIS PROJECT'S BASE RATE IS 0.263, i.e. ABOVE the p=0.2 regime where the paper reportedly finds no advantage. Provisional conclusion: this evidence does NOT support switching the primary target from direct binary classification to regression-then-threshold or a distributional head. It would only argue for the switch at a much rarer threshold (a 20-30 mg/L alarm, or a rare site-specific percentile). Tier-3, and note the 0.65 figure is reportedly READ OFF A FIGURE, not tabulated — the paper reportedly publishes results only as log-scale figures.
findings.effectSize: Reported: PSS_1/PSS_2 ~1.0 at p=0.2, ~0.65 at p=0.002 (1-hour-ahead wind); BSS_2 stays positive as p decreases while BSS_1 degrades sharply. Wind thresholds p in {0.2 ... 0.002}, rainfall p in {0.5 ... 0.025}. No exact numeric tables; 0.65 is approximate.
findings.splitProtocol: random-split — random partition of CALENDAR DAYS into 85/10/5 train/val/test, day-blocked with a 17:00 UTC cutoff to block within-day autocorrelation. This is a TEMPORAL random split, NOT spatial holdout; every test station was in training. NOT comparable to LOFO AUC 0.820.
findings.nBasins: 278 wind stations / 268 rainfall stations (MeteoNet, southeastern France, 2016-2018), ~3.5-4.1e6 samples — meteorological stations, not basins.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The comparison is between two estimators on a pooled sample and says nothing about spatial degrees of freedom. Its evidence base of 278 stations is >>19, but since the conclusion for this project is 'no change needed', the n mismatch does not create a false hope — it just means the paper cannot license a change either way here.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO EVIDENCE. The paper reportedly trains a single pooled model with station lat/lon/altitude as contextual features — architecturally the same trick as this project's static geography — but NEVER evaluates transfer to an unseen station, because the split partitions days, not stations. It therefore provides ZERO evidence about the ungauged-pin setting.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT PREDICTS A DISTRIBUTIONAL REFORMULATION WOULD NOT FIX THIS PROJECT'S ACTUAL PROBLEM. Baggio & Muzy reportedly state that 'The specific parametric shape of the chosen distribution plays a secondary role compared to accurately capturing predictable shifts in its bulk properties (i.e., mean and variance)', interpreting extremes as conditional displacement of the whole distribution rather than intrinsic tail behavior. IF VERIFIED, the implication is sharp and unfavorable: the quantity that dominates exceedance skill is the conditional MEAN LEVEL, and failing to place the conditional mean of an unseen basin is EXACTLY this project's deficit (between_r2 0.21 against within_r2 0.42). A distributional or heteroscedastic two-head reformulation would inherit the same between-site error rather than repair it. The constructive residue: if a distributional head is ever built, invest in mean and variance per site-day, not in an exotic heavy-tailed family. Tier-3; the authors reportedly DEFER the sensitivity analysis across parametric families to future work, so even in the source this is asserted rather than fully quantified.
findings.effectSize: Qualitative; sensitivity analysis across parametric families explicitly deferred by the authors. No ablation numbers.
findings.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test
findings.feasibilityAtN19: A heteroscedastic two-head model is trainable on 160k rows, but the mean-level term it depends on is governed by ~19 independent between-site units. That is the binding constraint and this paper's theory does not address it at all.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The reformulation itself would deploy fine (needs no local history), but per this finding it would not close the gap that matters at an ungauged pin.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. Peaks-over-threshold / extreme value theory is reportedly a dead end for this target. Baggio & Muzy, in a 2026 paper whose entire subject is threshold-exceedance forecasting, reportedly considered and explicitly DECLINED EVT/GPD, citing threshold selection's 'notoriously difficult bias-variance trade-off', and fitted full-support parametric conditional laws instead (a three-parameter multifractal-Rice for wind, a zero-inflated mixed lognormal for rainfall). Reinforcing this from first principles: at a 26.3% base rate this project's violations are not in a tail regime at all, so POT machinery is prima facie the wrong tool. Note the evidential limitation honestly — no EVT baseline was reportedly run, so the paper offers a JUDGEMENT against POT, not a head-to-head number. Combined with the total absence of any water-quality POT/EVT source in this angle's corpus, the position 'EVT is not indicated for the primary 10 mg/L target' is reasonable but rests on unverified secondary evidence plus the base-rate argument.
findings.effectSize: Qualitative methodological rejection; no EVT-vs-distributional comparison was run, so no comparative number exists.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: Moot for the primary target. If a rare high-threshold alarm (e.g. 20-30 mg/L) were ever added, EVT would face both the threshold-selection problem AND n=19 between-site units — a combination with no supporting evidence anywhere in this corpus.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: not-applicable — not recommended for the primary target in any deployment setting.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, BUT ACTIONABLE AND SELF-CONTAINED. The exceedance-forecasting literature reportedly evaluates with a two-tier metric set — proper scoring rules on the probability output (Brier score, logarithmic score, reported as SKILL SCORES against a climatological reference, i.e. BSS) plus deterministic categorical skill scores after thresholding (Peirce Skill Score, Critical Success Index, Heidke Skill Score) — and reportedly does NOT use ROC-AUC or PR-AUC as headline metrics. Because these are referenced to a base-rate climatology, they are far more comparable across studies with different base rates than raw AUC. THIS PROJECT reports AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634, 2.41x lift, Brier 0.137, but no BSS/PSS/CSI/HSS — a concrete reason its numbers cannot currently be benchmarked against this literature. Adding them is a few lines of code on existing LOFO predictions. ARITHMETIC NOTE, FLAGGED AS OUR OWN DERIVATION AND NOT FROM ANY SOURCE: a climatological forecast at base rate 0.263 has Brier 0.263*0.737 = 0.1938, so Brier 0.137 implies BSS = 1 - 0.137/0.1938 = 0.293. That is a LOFO (spatial-holdout) number and must never be compared to the source paper's random-split figures. Tier-3 as to the claim that this metric set is the field standard.
findings.effectSize: Metric-set claim, no performance number attached. Derived BSS ~0.293 is our own arithmetic from our Brier 0.137 and base rate 0.263.
findings.splitProtocol: Source numbers: random-split (day-blocked). Our derived BSS 0.293: spatial-holdout (LOFO). THE TWO MUST NOT BE COMPARED.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — computing BSS/PSS/CSI/HSS from existing held-out predictions is free and n-independent. Report them per basin family as well as pooled, so the between-site spread is visible rather than averaged away.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — pure evaluation change, no data requirement.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. There is reportedly a peer-reviewed ES&T precedent for BOTH of this project's contested target choices. The beach study reportedly set its exceedance threshold at 50% OF THE REGULATORY VALUE (320 CCE/100 mL vs an EPA Beach Action Value of 640 for Chicago; 30 vs 60 CFU/100 mL for San Diego), justified as 'a more health-protective (conservative) level' and because 'neither Chicago nor San Diego beaches typically approach their respective BAVs' — i.e. the full regulatory threshold yielded too few positives to model. It also reportedly defined the outcome on SINGLE DAILY MEASUREMENTS with no averaging period. IF VERIFIED, this legitimizes (i) defining exceedance on a single daily statistic rather than a regulatory average, and (ii) moving the threshold as a normal modeling choice rather than a corruption of the target. Striking corroborating detail worth checking: the resulting base rates were reportedly 26.9% and 33.6%, bracketing this project's 0.263. Tier-3 unverified.
findings.effectSize: Reported: threshold set at 0.5x the Beach Action Value; resulting exceedance base rates 26.9% (Chicago) and 33.6% (San Diego).
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable — a target-definition precedent, not a method with a sample-size requirement.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES as a framing precedent. Note it cuts both ways: it licenses the current daily-max/10 mg/L construction AND licenses moving to a 5 mg/L target if that improves the between-site signal.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. A 5 mg/L (as N) classification target would reportedly be a genuine citable regulatory decision boundary, not an arbitrary alternative: 40 CFR 141.23(d)(2)-(3) is quoted as letting a surface water system reduce sampling 'to annually if all analytical results from four consecutive quarters are <50 percent of the MCL' and requiring a return to quarterly monitoring 'if any one sample is >=50 percent of the MCL'. IF VERIFIED, a 5 mg/L target has three properties worth testing: it is defensible regulatorily, it would have a substantially higher base rate than 0.263 (more positives per basin family), and higher per-site positive counts mean better-estimated site-level exceedance RATES — plausibly improving the between-site signal-to-noise that is this project's binding deficit. Corroborating context from the Iowa side, also unverified: the DNR ambient network's reported 2000-2009 median nitrate+nitrite was 5.8 ppm over ~9,500 grab samples, so 5 mg/L sits near the middle of the ambient distribution — good for class balance, though it also means a 5 mg/L 'alarm' is close to a coin flip statewide and would need careful product framing. Tier-3 on both the CFR quotation and the Iowa median.
findings.effectSize: Reported: regulatory monitoring-frequency trigger at 5 mg/L as N = 50% of MCL. Reported Iowa DNR ambient median nitrate+nitrite 5.8 ppm (~9,500 samples, 2000-2009), 75th percentile >3.0 ppm.
findings.nBasins: not-applicable (CFR); ~9,500 Iowa grab samples, number of distinct sites not stated in the source
findings.feasibilityAtN19: MODERATE-TO-GOOD. Does not create new independent basin families — still 19 — but raises positives per family, which tightens each family's exceedance-rate estimate. That is a real if modest improvement in the between-site regression's effective precision, and it is testable today by relabeling and rerunning LOFO. Run it as an ablation at 5, 8, 10 and 12 mg/L and report the between-site term at each.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — a pure relabeling of the target, no new data required.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT UNDERCUTS THE 'DAILY MAXIMUM' CHOICE SPECIFICALLY. Two identical in situ UV-Vis spectrophotometers (s::can spectro::lyser) installed side-by-side in the same stream reportedly disagreed substantially on SUB-DAILY nitrate structure — Pearson r between the two sensors' deviations-from-background of only 0.429, 0.454 and 0.813 at three sites while in parallel position — whereas the SAME paired sensors reportedly agreed at r > 0.98 for dissolved organic carbon at all three. IF VERIFIED, the within-day component of a UV-Vis nitrate record is only weakly reproducible between instruments, so a DAILY MAXIMUM inherits instrument-specific noise that a daily mean or median would average out. This is the strongest argument in the angle for testing a daily-MEAN or daily-MEDIAN label as an alternative to daily-max — a cheap ablation on existing data. Tier-3; note the study is 4 tropical Kenyan headwater/mixed catchments (27-36 km2 sub-catchments plus a 1021 km2 outlet), Nov 2014-Oct 2019, 10-minute sampling — a different climate, scale and nitrate regime from tile-drained Iowa, so transferability of the magnitude is itself unestablished.
findings.effectSize: Reported: nitrate inter-sensor r = 0.43-0.81 vs DOC r > 0.98 in parallel position; under shading treatment nitrate r = 0.657 / 0.505 / 0.236 vs DOC r > 0.8 at all sites.
findings.nBasins: 4 catchments, Kenya (3 nested sub-catchments 27-36 km2 + a 1021 km2 outlet); paired mobile-sensor comparison at 3 of the 4 sites.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable to the claim itself. The implied action — relabel with daily mean/median and rerun LOFO — is fully feasible at n=19 and costs one training run.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — a label-construction change on the training data; the deployed model is unaffected in its inputs.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT QUANTIFIES WHEN 'DAILY MAX' IS INDEFENSIBLE. The manufacturer-stated accuracy of the s::can spectro::lyser nitrate measurement at 5 mm path length is reportedly '±2% + 0.2 mg N/L' over 0-60 mg N/L, and the authors reportedly warn against interpreting diurnal patterns 'when the diurnal variations are of the same order of magnitude as sensor accuracy or resolution.' IF VERIFIED, this gives a decision rule with a number attached: at 10 mg N/L the instrument uncertainty is roughly ±0.4 mg N/L, so site-days whose daily max falls within ~0.4 mg/L of the 10 mg/L threshold have effectively coin-flip label assignment. Directly actionable on the existing dataset: compute what fraction of the 160,074 site-days sit in the 9.6-10.4 mg/L band, and report model performance with those rows excluded as a label-noise sensitivity check — if that band holds a large share of the errors, some of the apparent performance ceiling is irreducible label noise rather than model deficiency. Tier-3; the spec should be confirmed against s::can documentation, and the relevant instrument for IWQIS/USGS Iowa sites must be identified rather than assumed to be this one.
findings.effectSize: Reported: ±2% + 0.2 mg N/L nitrate accuracy; 220-720 nm, 2.5 nm resolution, 5 mm path length, 10-min interval. Implies ~±0.4 mg N/L at the 10 mg/L threshold.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — a label-noise sensitivity analysis on existing rows, independent of the number of basin families.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — affects training-label quality and reported performance, not deployment inputs.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, BUT IT LARGELY EXONERATES THE DAILY-MAX CHOICE ON MAGNITUDE GROUNDS — PARTIALLY CONTRADICTING THE TWO FINDINGS ABOVE, WHICH SHOULD BE NOTED AS AN INTERNAL TENSION IN THIS ANGLE. The same study reportedly compiles published diurnal nitrate amplitudes spanning three orders of magnitude: 0.01-0.15 mg N/L in temperate/subtropical rivers in the US, Spain and UK; 0.4-0.6 mg N/L in other UK rivers; 1.5 mg N/L in a Mediterranean headwater; with its own Kenyan amplitudes up to 0.25 mg N/L at low flow and <0.02 mg N/L at high flow. It also reportedly finds diurnal amplitude DECREASING monotonically with discharge class at all four sites while background concentration INCREASES with discharge. IF VERIFIED, two things follow. First, in the typical temperate agricultural case the daily-max-minus-daily-mean gap is roughly 0.005-0.3 mg N/L — small against a 10 mg/L threshold — so the max-vs-mean choice is unlikely to move many labels. Second and more usefully, that gap is SMALLEST exactly on high-flow days when concentrations and exceedance risk are highest, so switching to daily mean should have least effect on the POSITIVE class and most effect on low-flow negatives. Reconcile against the inter-sensor-reproducibility finding: amplitude may be small AND poorly reproducible at once, which would make daily max mostly harmless but never preferable.
findings.effectSize: Reported amplitudes: 0.01-0.15 mg N/L (US/Spain/UK), 0.4-0.6 (UK rivers), 1.5 (Mediterranean headwater), <=0.25 (this study, low flow), <0.02 (this study, high flow). Reported background nitrate rising with flow: SHA 0.52 -> 0.89 -> 1.30 mg N/L; TTP 1.17 -> 1.74 -> 2.21; OUT 0.65 -> 0.84 -> 0.99 across low/medium/high flow classes (Q70/Q30).
findings.nBasins: Literature compilation across ~6 cited studies plus the 4 Kenyan catchments; individual study n not stated in the source.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable. The implied check — measure the actual daily-max-minus-daily-mean distribution in the Iowa sensor records — is directly computable and requires no external data at all. DO THIS FIRST: it settles the max-vs-mean question empirically on this project's own data and makes the Kenyan transferability question irrelevant.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — label-construction analysis only.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT IDENTIFIES A TESTABLE BIAS ON EXACTLY THE HIGHEST-RISK DAYS. The same study reportedly cites multiple prior works establishing turbidity thresholds above which UV-Vis sensors cannot provide valid nitrate measurements — >80 FTU, >300-450 FTU, and >1000 NTU depending on the study — and notes this is 'especially problematic' where rainfall causes short sharp turbidity spikes. IF VERIFIED, and because high-turbidity storm periods coincide with the runoff events that drive nitrate exceedance, this predicts a SYSTEMATIC, NON-RANDOM measurement gap or bias in sensor-derived daily maxima precisely on the days the model most needs to get right. DIRECTLY TESTABLE ON DATA ALREADY ON DISK: co-located turbidity exists at 61 of 85 sites. Check whether nitrate observations are preferentially missing, flagged, or biased on days exceeding these turbidity levels, and whether daily-max labels are disproportionately unreliable then. If confirmed in the Iowa data, this is missing-not-at-random on the positive class — a label-quality problem that would depress apparent performance and that no amount of feature engineering can fix. Tier-3 (and the thresholds are themselves second-hand citations within the source, so they are two removes from verification).
findings.effectSize: Reported turbidity invalidity thresholds for UV-Vis nitrate: >80 FTU, >300-450 FTU, >1000 NTU across three cited studies (attributed to Huebsch et al. 2015 HESS, Kamari et al. 2018 J. Hydrol., Lee et al. 2015 Biogeosciences).
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — uses on-disk co-located turbidity at 61 sites; it is a data-quality audit, not a modeling method, so the 19-family limit does not bind.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The AUDIT works and matters (it changes what training labels are trusted). The turbidity variable itself is NOT available at an arbitrary pin and must not become a model feature.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT SUPPORTS THE 'DAY-LEVEL BINARY' CONSTRUCTION WHILE COMPLICATING THE 'MAXIMUM' PART. Two reportedly opposing CFR provisions bear on the averaging period. On one side, 40 CFR 141.23(i)(3) is quoted as making nitrate one of the few SDWA contaminants judged on a SINGLE sample — 'Compliance with the maximum contaminant levels for nitrate and nitrate is determined based on one sample if the levels of these contaminants are below the MCLs' — which supports an event-level daily framing over a smoothed one, consistent with this project's own finding that 3-day/7-day rolling smoothed targets performed worse. On the other side, 141.23(f)(2) and (i)(3) are quoted as requiring a confirmation sample within 24 hours when an exceedance is indicated, with 'compliance ... determined based on the average of the initial and confirmation samples' — making the operative regulatory statistic a 24-hour TWO-SAMPLE MEAN conditional on an initial exceedance, not a maximum. IF VERIFIED, the current daily-max label is systematically MORE permissive of positives than the regulatory statistic, i.e. it over-declares violations relative to how compliance would actually be determined. Tier-3 on both quotations.
findings.effectSize: Reported: n=1 sample compliance basis when below the MCL, versus annual-average basis for other inorganics in 141.23(i)(1)-(2); confirmation-sample averaging window 24 hours over 2 samples.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable. The implied ablation — relabel using a daily mean, or a 'max-then-confirm' two-statistic rule — is one training run.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — label construction only. NOTE the framing constraint from the Class C finding: these CFR provisions govern treated water at a distribution entry point, so they are an ANALOGY for raw stream water, not a governing rule.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED. A basic but high-consequence unit check: 40 CFR 141.62(b) reportedly expresses the nitrate MCL AS NITROGEN — the table is quoted as reading '(7) Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen)', '(8) Nitrite | 1 (as Nitrogen)', '(9) Total Nitrate and Nitrite | 10 (as Nitrogen)'. A sensor reporting nitrate as the NO3 ion rather than NO3-N differs by a factor of 4.43. This makes the entire label definition falsifiable by a five-minute check of IWQIS and USGS parameter codes and units against the CFR basis. DO THIS CHECK REGARDLESS of whether the CFR citation verifies — a units error here would silently invalidate the target, the 0.263 base rate, and every performance number in the project. The reported Iowa ambient median of 5.8 ppm nitrate+nitrite is a useful sanity anchor: an as-NO3 record would sit ~4.4x higher.
findings.effectSize: Reported: MCL = 10 mg/L as N; 4.43x conversion factor if a record is in NO3-ion units.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable — a units audit of existing data.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: not-applicable, but it is a precondition for the target being meaningful anywhere.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THIS PROJECT'S BASE RATE CANNOT BE COMPARED TO PUBLISHED EXCEEDANCE RATES. 40 CFR 141.23(d)(1) is reportedly quoted as establishing quarterly (surface water) or annual (groundwater) nitrate sampling, with NO provision anywhere in the section addressing continuous, high-frequency, or daily sensor measurements. IF VERIFIED, the regulatory record against which any historical 'violation rate' was judged is built from ~4 grab samples per year, whereas this project's label is ~365 daily sensor maxima per year — roughly a 90x frequency mismatch. Consequence: the 0.263 base rate is NOT comparable to any published regulatory exceedance rate, and the reported gap between it and the Iowa ambient grab-sample median of 5.8 mg/L plausibly reflects (a) daily-max vs grab-sample statistics and (b) sensor-site selection toward high-nitrate agricultural basins. Both are testable on existing data by subsampling the sensor records to a quarterly grab schedule and recomputing the exceedance rate — a direct measurement of this project's own sampling-frequency bias. This is the only concrete purchase the angle obtained on the sampling-frequency-bias question; no source in the corpus addresses it directly.
findings.effectSize: Reported: 4 samples/year (surface water) or 1/year (groundwater) regulatory frequency vs ~365 daily maxima in the project label; ~90x mismatch.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — the subsampling experiment runs on existing per-site sensor records. With 19 families it also yields a per-family estimate of how much the sensor-vs-grab statistic shifts the apparent exceedance rate, which feeds directly into the between-site rate-prediction target.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — a characterization of the training label, not a deployment input.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, BUT IT IS THE ONE AGENCY PRECEDENT FOR THIS PROJECT'S EXACT LABEL CONSTRUCTION. Iowa DNR reportedly built a separate methodology for continuous sensor data because grab-sample methods 'are not directly applicable' to 24-hour sensor records, and — for DISSOLVED OXYGEN only — defines a violation as 'a day where levels of dissolved oxygen failed to remain above the 16-hour criterion for at least 16 hours' or 'a day (24-hour period) when the dissolved oxygen falls below the 24-hour criterion', then applies the same 10%-of-days binomial rule. IF VERIFIED, two implications. (1) The project's 'reduce continuous sensor data to a daily binary flag' construction MATCHES the agency's own reduction of continuous data, which supports the target's construction — though note it is a precedent for DO, not for nitrate, and the reduction used is a DURATION-BASED rule (below criterion for >=16 hours), not a simple daily extremum. A duration-based nitrate label ('above 10 mg/L for >=16 hours') is therefore an agency-shaped alternative worth an ablation, and would be far more robust to the inter-sensor sub-daily noise flagged elsewhere in this angle than a daily maximum is. (2) The agency reportedly requires the >10%-of-days condition to RECUR IN TWO DIFFERENT YEARS within five years before listing, explicitly guarding against single-year weather anomalies — a robustness criterion the per-day label does not encode.
findings.effectSize: Reported: 28-day deployment; >10% of monitored days in violation; must recur in 2 different years within a 5-year period; Lin et al. (2000) binomial at >90% CL.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH for the duration-based relabeling ablation (needs sub-daily nitrate records, which exist). The two-years-in-five recurrence criterion is harder: it consumes record length rather than sites, and sites with short records could not be assessed under it — see the Lin binomial finding.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — both the duration label and the multi-year rate target are computed from predictions and need no local history.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND USEFUL FOR HONEST UNCERTAINTY REPORTING ON PER-SITE RATES. Iowa DNR's binomial small-sample correction (Lin et al. 2000, as tabulated by NDEQ 2006) reportedly specifies exact exceedance counts required to declare impairment at >90% confidence: n=10 requires 3 exceedances (CL 0.930); n=12 requires 4 (0.974); n=19 requires 5 (0.965); n=25 requires 5 (0.902); n=40 requires 7 (0.900); n=50 requires 9 (0.942); n=75 requires 12 (0.931); n=100 requires 15 (0.927). The required exceedance FRACTION is reportedly far above the nominal 10% at small n (3/10 = 30%, 5/25 = 20%), converging toward 15% only at n=100. IF VERIFIED, this is an agency-sanctioned uncertainty rule applicable directly to per-site sensor records and to model-PREDICTED exceedance rates, and it quantifies how many observations a site needs before its rate is even estimable. Relevant because this project's sites vary greatly in record length: short-record sites carry rate estimates the regulator itself would refuse to act on, and those sites should probably be down-weighted or excluded when fitting or evaluating the between-site rate term. Tier-3, and note the numbers are a second-hand tabulation within the Iowa document.
findings.effectSize: Reported: n=10 -> 3 exceedances (CL 0.930); n=25 -> 5 (0.902); n=50 -> 9 (0.942); n=100 -> 15 (0.927); effective required fraction ~30% at n=10 falling to ~15% at n=100.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: HIGH — it is a table lookup applied to existing per-site records, and it directly improves the honesty of any n=19 between-site rate analysis by attaching a defensible confidence rule to each family's rate estimate.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES — applies to the predicted rate at any location, gauged or not.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED SCOPE/NEGATIVE FINDING about the corpus itself, reported so the gap is not silently absorbed. The Brenning et al. groundwater-mapping paper — the angle's main source on regression-then-threshold — reportedly does NOT address peaks-over-threshold/EVT for water quality, the regulatory definition or averaging period of the nitrate MCL, TMDL or ambient-stream operationalization as distinct from treated drinking water, sensor-derived daily statistics or sampling-frequency bias, or any published virtual-sensor AUC/PR-AUC benchmark for spatially held-out exceedance. It is reportedly a purely SPATIAL, static-snapshot GROUNDWATER mapping paper with no time-series component. Its transferable content is confined to the estimator-bias and area-calibration argument. Consequently the angle's coverage of its own commissioned questions is UNEVEN: question (a) rests on two papers neither of which is about water quality time series, and the request for comparable published virtual-sensor exceedance benchmarks came back essentially empty.
findings.effectSize: n/a — scope limitation of a source.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: not-applicable

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED CONTEXT FINDING, LOW PRIORITY FOR THE BETWEEN-SITE GAP. The beach FIB study reportedly summarizes prior-literature model sensitivity of 27-65% at Great Lakes sites and 28-30% at California beaches with specificity typically 85-99%, notes 'model sensitivity was generally better in models of FIB at rivers ... than at coastal waters', and reports that in its own results 'only four of the 12 models had sensitivity above 0.70.' IF VERIFIED, this project's LOFO recall of 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate (specificity 0.90) sits inside the upper half of that band, and AUC 0.820 exceeds every AUC in that paper (max 0.733, same-region training). USE WITH HEAVY CAUTION: the split protocols of the summarized prior studies are unknown, they are a different analyte, and the comparison is tier-3 — it is a rough sanity check that this project's numbers are not absurd, NOT a benchmark claim. Separately and more usefully: the beta=2 deployment setting (recall 0.864, 59% false alarms) pushes specificity far below the 0.85-0.99 the FIB literature holds, so it should be presented explicitly as a cost-sensitive public-health decision rather than as a performance result.
findings.effectSize: Reported prior-literature sensitivity 27-65% (Great Lakes), 28-30% (California beaches), specificity 85-99%; the paper's own max AUC 0.733.
findings.splitProtocol: unknown for the summarized prior studies — an aggregated literature table. The paper's own results are spatial-holdout at region level. Because the protocols are unknown, these numbers are NOT safely comparable to LOFO 0.820.
findings.nBasins: unknown for the summarized studies; 33 beaches for the paper's own results.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: not-applicable — external calibration context, not a method.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: not-applicable

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED, AND LARGELY NON-TRANSFERABLE — recorded to prevent a false lead. Brenning et al.'s reported modeling stack is trans-Gaussian regression-kriging combined with QUANTILE REGRESSION FORESTS under 'structured non-stationarity across hydrogeological districts' (district-level rather than one global model), with reported per-district linear-model R2 of 0.15-0.62 and semivariogram practical ranges of 0.3-22.3 km. The QRF component is the 'distributional-then-integrate' route in production alongside geostatistics. TWO CAUTIONS. (1) The reported spatial-correlation ranges of 0.3-22.3 km are for groundwater wells and are far shorter than typical Iowa inter-sensor distances, so the KRIGING half requires a spatially dense observation network and will NOT transfer to an arbitrary Iowa map pin whose nearest nitrate sensor may be tens of km away. Only the QRF + area-calibration half is deployable here. (2) The 'district-level model structure' idea is superficially attractive for the between-site problem, but with 19 independent basin families, splitting into regional sub-models would leave a handful of families per region — almost certainly infeasible. Flag any 'fit separate models per hydrologic region' proposal against the n=19 constraint before pursuing.
findings.effectSize: Reported: per-district linear-model R2 0.15-0.62; semivariogram practical ranges 0.3-22.3 km.
findings.feasibilityAtN19: LOW for the district-stratified structure — 19 families cannot support regional sub-models. MODERATE for a plain QRF/quantile head fitted globally, which uses all 160k rows, though per the Baggio & Muzy mean/variance finding it would inherit the same between-site error.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The kriging half: NO — requires a dense local observation network. The QRF half: YES.

datasets.name: Iowa DNR Water Quality Standards — designated use classifications (Class A/B/C/HH) for stream segments; the Class C 'source of a water supply' layer specifically
datasets.url: https://www.iowadnr.gov/environmental-protection/water-quality/water-monitoring/impaired-waters (assessment/designated-use GIS layers; the 2020 assessment methodology PDF is at https://publications.iowa.gov/35257/1/2020%20IA%20Methodology_Final.pdf)
datasets.resolution: Stream segment / assessment-unit polygons and lines, typically keyed to NHD reach codes
datasets.access: UNVERIFIED — believed to be free public download via the Iowa DNR GIS library / NRGIS shapefile service, plus the ArcGIS REST services Iowa DNR publishes. No authentication expected. The exact endpoint was NOT confirmed in this research and must be located before this is treated as operational.
datasets.license: UNVERIFIED — presumed public domain / open state government data. Confirm before redistribution.
datasets.coversMultiState: NO — Iowa only. This is acceptable because the use is to label the PIN's own segment, not to aggregate over the upstream basin, and the product is Iowa-scoped. Basins extending into Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, South Dakota or Illinois would have no designation for their out-of-state reaches, which does not matter for pin labeling.
datasets.whyUseful: Determines whether a 10 mg/L exceedance prediction at a given pin has any regulatory meaning. Per the (unverified) finding above, Iowa's nitrate criterion applies ONLY to Class C waters; elsewhere the label is a physical threshold with no legal status. Without this layer the product risks implying a regulatory violation where none is defined.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Not a model feature — a PRODUCT-LAYER LOOKUP. At pin resolution time, after NLDI returns the reach comid, join to the designated-use layer to retrieve the segment's use classes. Create the boolean `is_class_c` and surface it in the UI: if true, present the prediction as 'probability of exceeding Iowa's Class C drinking-water-source criterion'; if false, present it as 'probability of exceeding 10 mg/L, a physical threshold borrowed from the drinking-water MCL, which carries no regulatory designation for this segment.' Optionally also record `is_class_c` per training site to check whether the ~85 sensor sites are disproportionately on Class C waters, which would be a selection-bias finding in its own right.
datasets.limitations: The claim that nitrate applies only to Class C is TIER-3 UNVERIFIED and must be confirmed in the Iowa Water Quality Standards (567 IAC Chapter 61, Table 6) before any UI wording is built on it. Designations change between assessment cycles. The exact download endpoint is unconfirmed.

datasets.name: Iowa DNR ambient stream/river water quality monitoring network — nitrate grab-sample record (accessible via Iowa's AQuIA / STORET-WQX holdings and the federal Water Quality Portal)
datasets.url: https://www.waterqualitydata.us/ (Water Quality Portal, USGS/EPA/NWQMC — programmatic); Iowa AQuIA: https://programs.iowadnr.gov/aquia/
datasets.resolution: Point samples at fixed ambient network stations; roughly monthly to quarterly grab samples
datasets.years: Reported ~2000-2009 for the 9,500-sample statistic cited in the Iowa methodology document; the network and the Water Quality Portal holdings extend well beyond that in both directions
datasets.access: Water Quality Portal: free REST/bulk CSV download, no authentication (https://www.waterqualitydata.us/data/Result/search?statecode=US%3A19&characteristicName=Nitrate&mimeType=csv). AQuIA: free web query interface. Both free and public.
datasets.license: Public domain (US federal/state government data). Confirm attribution requirements for AQuIA.
datasets.coversMultiState: The Water Quality Portal covers ALL states, so the multi-state portions of basins ARE reachable by changing the statecode/bbox parameter — a genuine advantage over Iowa-only sources for basins extending into MN/MO/NE/SD/IL.
datasets.whyUseful: Two distinct uses, both aimed at the between-site gap. (1) EXTERNAL BASE-RATE CHECK: the Iowa methodology reportedly cites a 2000-2009 ambient median nitrate+nitrite of 5.8 ppm over ~9,500 samples with 75th percentile >3.0 ppm — far below the sensor network's 0.263 daily-max exceedance rate. Reconciling these quantifies how much of this project's base rate comes from daily-max-vs-grab statistics versus sensor-site selection toward high-nitrate agricultural basins. (2) POTENTIAL ADDITIONAL BETWEEN-SITE TRAINING UNITS: the ambient network has far more spatial coverage than the ~85 continuous sensors, and site-level exceedance RATES (the regulator's quantity) are estimable from sparse grab samples in a way that daily timing is not.
datasets.howToIncorporate: For (1): pull all Iowa nitrate results from the Water Quality Portal, compute the distribution of single-sample values, and compare against the sensor network's daily-max distribution subsampled to a quarterly schedule; report the gap decomposed into statistic effect and site-selection effect. For (2) — the more ambitious and more valuable use: for every ambient station with >=10 nitrate samples, delineate its upstream basin via NLDI exactly as for the sensor sites, build the SAME static feature vector (crop fractions, N-surplus, lat/lon, log basin area by distance bucket), and compute the station's empirical exceedance FRACTION at 10 mg/L with a Lin-et-al binomial confidence interval. This yields a second, much larger training set for a SITE-LEVEL RATE regression — the exact between-site target the model is worst at — with many more independent basins than 19. Feature name: unchanged static features; target: `exceedance_rate_10mgL` per station, weighted by sample count. This does not help the daily-timing model at all, but the timing model is already good.
datasets.limitations: Grab samples are biased relative to sensor daily maxima and are not synoptic with storm events, so the rate estimate is noisy per station — this is exactly what the Lin binomial correction is for. Sample counts per station vary enormously and many stations will fall below the n=10 minimum. Ambient stations are sited for regulatory representativeness, not to span the covariate space. Basin delineation for hundreds of new stations is a real engineering cost. AND CRITICALLY: the entire premise — that the regulator's quantity is a site-level rate — is TIER-3 UNVERIFIED. Verify the Iowa methodology first; this dataset expansion is only worth its cost if that framing holds.

datasets.name: 40 CFR Part 141 (National Primary Drinking Water Regulations), specifically 141.23 (inorganic monitoring) and 141.62 (MCLs for inorganic contaminants)
datasets.access: Free, public, no authentication; eCFR also offers a bulk XML/JSON API at https://www.ecfr.gov/developers/documentation/api/v1
datasets.license: US federal government work, public domain
datasets.coversMultiState: Federal — applies nationwide, so it covers the multi-state portions of basins as well as Iowa.
datasets.whyUseful: Establishes the units basis of the 10 mg/L threshold (reportedly 'as Nitrogen', with a 4.43x error risk if a sensor reports NO3 ion), the compliance averaging period (reportedly single-sample below the MCL, but a 24-hour two-sample mean once an exceedance is indicated), the 50%-of-MCL (5 mg/L) monitoring trigger that would make an alternative 5 mg/L target regulatorily citable, the treated-water compliance point that determines whether this project's raw-stream framing is an analogy rather than a regulation, and the quarterly sampling regime that makes the 0.263 base rate incomparable to published regulatory exceedance rates.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Not a model input — a TARGET-DEFINITION AUDIT and a product-copy source. Concretely: (a) verify IWQIS and USGS parameter codes and units for every nitrate series against the 'as Nitrogen' basis and fail loudly on any as-NO3 series; (b) add the 5 mg/L relabeling as a formal ablation arm alongside 8, 10 and 12 mg/L, reporting between_r2 and between_rate_r2 at each so the threshold choice is made on between-site evidence rather than convention; (c) use 141.23(a)(2) to write the product disclaimer distinguishing the raw-stream prediction from a compliance determination.
datasets.limitations: All CFR content in this angle is TIER-3 — the quotations came from the Cornell mirror via unverified extraction and must be re-read on eCFR, which is the authoritative source. Federal drinking-water regulations govern treated water at distribution entry points and have NO direct application to ambient streams, so they can inform the target's construction but cannot justify calling a stream prediction a 'violation'. State ambient standards (567 IAC Ch. 61) and the CWA 303(d)/TMDL framework are the relevant instruments for streams, and this angle did NOT retrieve the underlying Iowa administrative code.

datasets.name: Co-located turbidity records already on disk (61 of 85 sensor sites) — used as a label-quality covariate, not a model feature
datasets.url: Already present in the project's IWQIS/USGS holdings; upstream sources are https://waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis (parameter code 63680) and the IIHR IWQIS platform https://iwqis.iowawis.org/
datasets.resolution: Same sub-daily cadence as the nitrate sensors (typically 15-minute), point observations at the sensor site
datasets.years: Matches the existing 2008-2026 sensor record where present
datasets.access: Already downloaded. Refreshable free via NWIS web services (no authentication) and by request to IIHR for IWQIS series.
datasets.license: Public domain for USGS; IWQIS terms should be confirmed with IIHR.
datasets.coversMultiState: not-applicable — these are point observations at existing sensor sites, not a basin-aggregated layer.
datasets.whyUseful: Tests the (unverified) claim that UV-Vis nitrate measurements become invalid above turbidity thresholds reportedly in the 80 FTU to 1000 NTU range, and that this failure coincides with the storm runoff events that drive exceedance. If true, training labels are missing-not-at-random ON THE POSITIVE CLASS — a label-quality ceiling that no feature engineering can lift and that would partly explain the apparent performance limit.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Do NOT add turbidity as a model feature (it is unavailable at an arbitrary map pin and would break deployment). Instead build the DIAGNOSTIC flag `high_turbidity_day` = (daily max turbidity > 80 FTU / > 300 FTU / > 1000 NTU, evaluated at each threshold) per site-day, then: (1) test whether nitrate observations are disproportionately missing or QA-flagged on those days; (2) compare the daily-max nitrate distribution on high- vs low-turbidity days at matched discharge; (3) rerun the LOFO evaluation excluding high-turbidity site-days and report whether AUC/PR-AUC and the between-site terms move. A material move means measured performance is partly bounded by sensor validity, which should be reported alongside the headline numbers.
datasets.limitations: Only 61 of 85 sites have turbidity, and the 24 without cannot be audited. The turbidity thresholds are TIER-3 and are themselves second-hand citations within the source paper — two removes from verification — and are instrument- and manufacturer-specific; the actual instrument deployed at Iowa IWQIS and USGS nitrate sites has NOT been identified in this research and may not be the s::can spectro::lyser the thresholds derive from. FTU and NTU are not interchangeable units. Establish the instrument model first, then obtain that manufacturer's stated turbidity limit rather than importing these numbers.

refuted.item: Nothing in this angle was refuted, because nothing in this angle was verified.
refuted.detail: The tier-1 survived and tier-1 refuted lists are both EMPTY. Adversarial verification was cut before reaching A8. No claim here has been checked against its primary source, and consequently no claim has been knocked down either. The absence of entries in this list is NOT evidence that the claims withstood scrutiny — it is evidence that scrutiny never happened. Treat every finding above as a lead requiring verification, not as a result.

refuted.item: PROVISIONALLY ARGUED AGAINST (not refuted — the argument itself is unverified): switching the primary target from direct binary classification to regression-then-threshold or a distributional-then-integrate formulation.
refuted.detail: The reported evidence places the distributional approach's advantage at rare exceedance probabilities (p << 0.2), with the two approaches essentially equivalent at moderate p. This project's base rate is 0.263. Separately, the reported mean-and-variance-dominate finding implies a distributional head would inherit the same between-site error that constitutes essentially all remaining headroom. Both arguments rest on a single unverified 2026 arXiv preprint whose numbers were reportedly read off log-scale figures rather than tables. Do not treat 'the current target is fine' as settled; treat it as the current best guess pending verification.

refuted.item: PROVISIONALLY ARGUED AGAINST (unverified): peaks-over-threshold / extreme value theory for the 10 mg/L target.
refuted.detail: A 26.3% base rate is not a tail, and the one 2026 exceedance-forecasting paper located reportedly considered and declined EVT/GPD over threshold-selection bias-variance concerns — but reportedly ran no EVT baseline, so there is no head-to-head number anywhere in this corpus. The angle also located NO water-quality POT/EVT literature at all (see uncovered), so this position rests on a base-rate argument plus one unverified secondary judgement.

refuted.item: RULED OUT FOR THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET (on unverified evidence, but on a structural rather than empirical basis): supervised transfer learning to improve exceedance prediction at new sites.
refuted.detail: The reported gains require labeled exceedance observations at the target site, which an arbitrary map pin with no nitrate history does not have. This disqualification follows from the method's definition, not from a contested measurement, so it is robust to the tier-3 status of the surrounding numbers. The deployment-legal alternative (unsupervised domain adaptation via CORAL) reportedly never improved over plain zero-shot generalization. Supervised TL remains potentially useful for a DIFFERENT product — onboarding a newly instrumented site after it accumulates observations — and that distinction must be stated prominently wherever TL is discussed.

refuted.item: FLAGGED AS LIKELY INFEASIBLE AT n=19: fitting separate regional/district sub-models, as in the reported hydrogeological-district structure of the groundwater paper.
refuted.detail: With 19 independent basin families, partitioning into regional sub-models leaves a handful of families per region. The reported evidence for district-stratified structure comes from a dense national well network. Any 'fit per hydrologic region' proposal must be checked against this constraint before it is pursued.

refuted.item: FLAGGED AS NOT DEPLOYABLE: the kriging / geostatistical half of the reported groundwater exceedance-mapping stack.
refuted.detail: Reported semivariogram practical ranges of 0.3-22.3 km are far shorter than typical Iowa inter-sensor distances, and kriging requires a spatially dense observation network near the prediction point. At an arbitrary Iowa pin the nearest nitrate sensor may be tens of km away. Only the quantile-regression-forest and area-calibration components of that method are candidates here.

uncovered.gap: PUBLISHED VIRTUAL-SENSOR EXCEEDANCE BENCHMARKS UNDER SPATIAL HOLDOUT — the specific deliverable requested, so that LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 / 2.41x lift could be compared to something rather than to nothing.
uncovered.detail: NOT FOUND. The angle produced exactly one spatially-held-out exceedance-classification comparator (beach fecal indicator bacteria: zero-shot cross-region AUC 0.567 and 0.482 against same-region 0.733 and 0.607), and it is a different analyte, a different response timescale, and a far coarser spatial unit (n=2 effective transfer units). No stream-nitrate, no water-quality, and no ungauged-basin exceedance-classification benchmark was retrieved. This project's headline numbers therefore STILL have no proper external benchmark. This is a live deficiency and should be the top priority for any follow-up search — suggested targets: the CAMELS/Caravan ungauged-basin literature for water-quality extensions, LSTM PUB (prediction in ungauged basins) papers that report classification rather than NSE, and the USGS/NWQP nitrate-load-estimation literature.

uncovered.gap: PEAKS-OVER-THRESHOLD / EXTREME VALUE THEORY APPLIED TO WATER QUALITY — question (a) asked directly whether EVT is used for water quality.
uncovered.detail: NO WATER-QUALITY EVT SOURCE WAS FOUND AT ALL. The only EVT-relevant evidence in the corpus is a meteorological paper's reported decision NOT to use it. The angle can say 'EVT appears unnecessary at a 26.3% base rate' on base-rate reasoning, but it CANNOT say what the water-quality literature does with POT/EVT, because no such source was retrieved. Absence of evidence, reported as absence.

uncovered.gap: TMDL AND 303(d) OPERATIONALIZATION OF NITRATE EXCEEDANCE FOR STREAMS — explicitly requested, and only partially covered.
uncovered.detail: The Iowa DNR 2020 assessment methodology (unverified) supplies the 303(d) LISTING rule — a three-year frequency-of-exceedance test with 10% and 25% cut points. But NO TMDL document was retrieved: nothing on how a nitrate TMDL sets load allocations, what averaging period or design flow condition it uses, or how a modeled daily exceedance probability would map onto TMDL practice. The underlying Iowa administrative code (567 IAC Chapter 61) was also NOT retrieved — the entire Iowa regulatory picture rests on one secondary methodology PDF, itself unverified. Follow-up should obtain 567 IAC Ch. 61 Table 6 directly and at least one Iowa nitrate TMDL.

uncovered.gap: SAMPLING-FREQUENCY BIAS IN SENSOR-DERIVED DAILY STATISTICS — requested, and only obliquely covered.
uncovered.detail: No source was found that directly studies how daily statistics derived from high-frequency nitrate sensors compare to grab-sample-based exceedance statistics, which is the literature the question asked for. What the angle obtained instead is (a) an inference from the reported CFR quarterly sampling regime that a ~90x frequency mismatch exists, and (b) a reported Iowa ambient grab-sample median of 5.8 mg/L to reconcile against the 0.263 sensor-based rate. Both are indirect. The good news is that this project can MEASURE its own sampling-frequency bias directly by subsampling its sensor records to a quarterly schedule, which is more informative than the missing literature would have been.

uncovered.gap: HEAD-TO-HEAD REGRESSION-THEN-THRESHOLD VS DIRECT CLASSIFICATION IN A WATER-QUALITY TIME SERIES.
uncovered.detail: The two sources bearing on question (a) are a static groundwater spatial-mapping study and a meteorological wind/rainfall nowcasting study. NEITHER is a water-quality time series, and neither is spatially held out in a way comparable to LOFO. The beach study reportedly built only direct classifiers and ran no regression comparison, so it establishes the field NORM but not a tested choice. The methodological fork this angle was commissioned to resolve has therefore NOT been resolved on in-domain evidence.

uncovered.gap: WHETHER DAILY MAXIMUM IS THE RIGHT DAILY STATISTIC, ANSWERED WITH IOWA DATA.
uncovered.detail: The angle assembled indirect and partly CONFLICTING evidence: daily maxima reportedly inherit poorly-reproducible sub-daily instrument noise (inter-sensor r 0.43-0.81 for nitrate versus >0.98 for DOC), yet reported diurnal amplitudes in temperate agricultural rivers (0.01-0.6 mg N/L) are small against a 10 mg/L threshold and reportedly shrink further at high flow when exceedance risk is greatest. All of it comes from four tropical Kenyan catchments and a literature compilation, with no Iowa or Corn Belt evidence whatsoever. This tension is resolvable ONLY on this project's own data: compute the distribution of daily-max minus daily-mean nitrate across the 160,074 site-days, count how many labels would flip, and rerun LOFO with a daily-mean, daily-median, and duration-based ('above 10 mg/L for >=16 hours', per the reported Iowa DO precedent) label. That experiment should be run before any further literature search on this sub-question.

uncovered.gap: THE ENTIRE ANGLE'S EVIDENTIARY FOUNDATION — no verification pass was run.
uncovered.detail: Restating this as an explicit coverage gap so it is not lost among the findings. Zero of the 34 upstream extractions were adversarially verified. The corpus's characteristic failure mode is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE — a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed — and this angle contains several structures that fit that profile exactly: an 80-98% effect size extracted from an abstract behind a 403, approximate skill-score ratios read off log-scale figures, regulatory language quoted from a mirror rather than the authoritative eCFR, and instrument thresholds cited second-hand within a secondary source. VERIFICATION PRIORITY ORDER, cheapest and highest-consequence first: (1) the nitrate units basis, as-N versus as-NO3, in this project's own data — a units error would invalidate everything; (2) Iowa's Class C designated-use restriction and the three-year 10%-rule, which carry the angle's single most important finding and its most serious legal-framing risk; (3) the CFR quotations, verifiable free on eCFR in minutes; (4) the beach-study transfer numbers, the only spatial-holdout comparator; (5) the Brenning 80-98% figure, which needs full-text access via interlibrary loan or an author request.
